purpose: Preserve investigated candidates that should not yet become territorial-practice claims, so later research does not repeatedly rediscover or overstate the same evidence.

candidates.reason: Specialist reassessment warns that an external Middle Nile slave trade is substantially less secure for earlier periods than older historiography often assumed. Do not project medieval/post-medieval patterns backward without bounded ancient status or captive evidence.

sources.title: Slavery and Slaving in the Medieval and Post-Medieval Kingdoms of the Middle Nile
sources.author: David N. Edwards
sources.version: British Academy / Oxford Academic chapter, 2011, pp. 79–108
sources.limitation: The chapter's direct empirical focus is medieval and post-medieval; it is used here to block retrospective assumptions, not to establish an ancient absence.

candidates.next_evidence_needed: Ancient Kushite/Meroitic evidence that directly establishes enslaved status, alienability, forced dependency, or an explicitly identified enslavement process in a bounded place/time.

candidates.reason: Reviewed work supports trans-Saharan connectivity, but the evidence inspected does not securely establish territorial slavery. Possible movement of enslaved people through exchange networks is insufficient for a territorial-practice classification.
candidates.next_evidence_needed: Specialist synthesis plus bounded textual or archaeological evidence distinguishing enslaved status from generic trade, dependency, or captive-taking.

candidates.candidate: Opone and the northern Somali coast
candidates.reason: The mid-first-century Periplus directly reports slaves exported from Opone to Egypt in increasing numbers and rarer slave exports from Malao. This is strong evidence for participation of specific Horn of Africa ports in slave trading, but it does not identify the captives' origins, acquisition mechanisms, or local legal/social status. Under the atlas methodology, trade-node evidence must not be converted mechanically into a territorial slavery-practice P-level.

sources.title: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
sources.author: Anonymous merchant; Wilfred H. Schoff translation
sources.limitation: A merchant itinerary records commodities and ports, not the local institutions or origins by which exported people became enslaved.

sources.title: Nomads Trading with Empires: Intercultural Trade in Ancient Somaliland in the First to Seventh Centuries CE
sources.author: Alfredo González-Ruibal et al.
sources.version: American Journal of Archaeology 126.1 (2022), published online 17 December 2021
sources.limitation: Establishes the northern Somali coast and its communities within the western Indian Ocean exchange system; it does not by itself establish local slavery institutions.

candidates.next_evidence_needed: A dedicated trade/event representation in the atlas data model, or independent bounded evidence for local enslavement/status practices at Opone/Malao. Until then, preserve this as strong slave-trade evidence without assigning a territorial P-level.

candidates.reason: The Periplus is the key first-century source for Rhapta and Azania, but the inspected scholarship notes slaves as an export from Opone rather than from Azania specifically. Do not spread Opone's evidence southward to Rhapta or the broader East African coast.

sources.title: Rhapta: the Location and Importance of East Africa's first Port
sources.author: B. A. Datoo
sources.limitation: Rhapta's exact location remains disputed and the article is not a slavery study.

candidates.next_evidence_needed: Independent source-native or specialist evidence specifically tying Rhapta/Azania to slave export, enslavement, or enslaved status rather than inference from the wider Indian Ocean network.
